newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: FOCUS-Venezuela sees gain from OPEC's loss.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Venezuela sees gain from OPEC's loss.

text.p: If Venezuela's delegation arrives at this year's OPEC meeting with a bounce in its step, it will be because, unlike some fellow-OPEC members, Venezuela expects to increase its oil revenues this year -- despite falling prices.

Venezuela is trying to force the pace of change in the organisation that once took the west hostage with a $40 barrel of oil. Its lone postion: maintain the group's market share, even if it means a lower price.

Unlike OPEC heavyweights Saudi Arabia and Kuwait, which are both holding back spare capacity, Venezuela is hiking its oil output by about 300,000 barrels per day this year to 3.245 million bpd, 40 percent above its official OPEC quota.
According to state oil company Petroleos de Venezuela (PDVSA) figures, Venezuela plans to pump 3.652 million bpd next year and 4.097 million bp in 1999.

If output rises as planned, Venezuela can afford to see world prices fall by 10 percent a year and still increase annual income. So far this year, Venezuela's average oil export price has fallen 7.7 percent to $16.97 versus $18.39 in 1996.

OPEC is expected to keep its long-ignored production ceiling of 25 million bpd unchanged at Wednesday's meeting, but this year Venezuela's Energy and Mines Minister Erwin Arrieta has called for a reality check.
"Because OPEC has concentrated exclusively on quotas and prices, it has allowed others to occupy the space (in the market) that we are leaving empty," he said last week.
He will demand a reply to his proposal last year that OPEC change its approach to the market.
PDVSA president Luis Giusti called last week for the group to scrap its system of output quotas altogether.
"That is sensible only if you have very large reserves and a low cost of production," a foreign banker in Venezuela said.
"It doesn't matter if you are selling oil or cigarettes, it never makes sense for a market leader to hold onto price and lose market share," he added.
With the sixth largest oil reserves in the world and a production cost of about $1.00 per barrel, PDVSA would be one of the last producers to shut wells in a price war.
Some see Venezuela's stance as disingenuous, benefiting from Saudi discipline while it hikes its own output. But others say Venezuela is leading the way to long-term survival of the group.
Analysts predict world oil demand will grow about two percent per year for the next decade or so, and only OPEC has the reserves to fulfil this demand.
"Venezuela is getting OPEC to look outwards, to look at forming strategic associations with distribution chains and getting access to finance its expansion," the banker said.

By 2006, PDVSA hopes to produce 6.3 million bpd, with two thirds of this coming from ventures involving private capital. It is already the biggest supplier of gasoline in the United States, through its Unoven and Citgo subsidiaries.

"Venezuela would argue that it is better to do that and develop its industry and increase production capacity than run the risk of being squeezed out of the market by other producers," the banker said.
